g.text: Watch only your immediate predecessor - and a release under a 10,000-deep queue wakes ONE waiter
Not the lock-holder's node, not every other waiter's. That single choice is the entire fairness-and-scale mechanism.
The lock queue, and who watches whom
HOLDS THE LOCK
waiting
exists(watch=true)
waiting
exists(watch=true)
waiting
exists(watch=true)
Each waiter watches exactly ONE node: the one immediately ahead of it. So a release fires exactly one notification, to exactly
one waiter, in strict arrival order - and a 10,000-deep queue releases with one wake-up rather than 10,000. Watching the
HOLDER instead would wake every waiter on every release: a thundering herd proportional to queue depth.
the fencing token IS the sequence number: fencingToken = parseSequenceNumber(myPath) -> 12
No separate token-issuing step is needed. The leader already assigns those numbers monotonically, as part of the single
globally-ordered write path - so acquire() just SURFACES the number the coordination service was already generating. Whatever
downstream resource the lock protects should receive that token with every write and REJECT any write carrying a lower token
than the highest it has already seen. That is where a real system's fencing token actually comes from, rather than a value
invented at the call site.
acquire(), and the one branch that looks like a bug and is not
DistributedLock.acquire(lockPath):
myPath = client.create(lockPath + '/lock-', data=sessionId,
mode=EPHEMERAL_SEQUENTIAL) # server assigns the number
while true:
children = client.getChildren(lockPath, watch=false)
sorted = sort(children) # purely numeric on the suffix
if myPath == sorted[0]:
return LockHandle(myPath,
fencingToken=parseSequenceNumber(myPath))
predecessor = sorted[indexOf(myPath) - 1] # the ONE node ahead of me
watchResult = client.exists(lockPath + '/' + predecessor, watch=true)
if watchResult is null:
continue # already gone - recheck NOW, do not wait for a
# watch event that will never fire
waitForWatchEvent() # ONE-SHOT: fires once, then must be re-set
# loop: re-list children, re-check whether I am now lowest
getChildren -> exists(watch=true) is NOT atomic - two separate round trips - and
that is worth stating plainly rather than reaching for a lock to close the gap.
It does not need one. The one place atomicity actually matters - assigning each
waiter a strictly ordered sequence number - is already pushed down into the
coordination service's own write path, the one place that can provide it for
free. So the continue-on-null-watch branch is not a workaround for a missing
lock; it is the correct response to a real, expected race the design already
accounts for.
The one place an in-process guard IS worth adding: a LockHandle called from two
threads of the SAME client process. That is a single-process reentrancy problem,
not a distributed one - a lightweight local guard is the right tool. Do not reach
for a distributed coordination primitive to solve a problem entirely within one
process.
SessionState as an enforced enum, not a connected: bool
CONNECTING
CONNECTED
EXPIRED
CLOSED
one-way TERMINAL transition
A client library that reconnects after EXPIRED gets a BRAND-NEW session, never a resumed one - and must treat every ephemeral
node and every watch it previously held as gone. Modelling that as an enforced enum rather than a boolean is what makes 'a
client can never assume its old session's ephemeral nodes still exist after expiry' a CHECKABLE RULE instead of a convention
every caller has to remember.
Three error cases designed for deliberately
the predecessor is deleted between getChildren and exists(watch=true)
a real and common race: the node immediately ahead is released in the gap. exists() returning 'not found' here is NOT an
error - it means the wait condition already resolved, so the loop rechecks immediately instead of waiting on a watch event
that will never arrive, because nothing is watching a node that no longer exists.
create() times out with no response
genuinely ambiguous - the same shape as a payments processor call: the leader may have committed the create and failed over
before the ack reached the client. Blindly retrying is UNSAFE, because it could produce a SECOND sequential node for the same
logical attempt, leaving the client waiting behind its own abandoned node. The safe recovery is embedding a client-generated
identifier (the session id) in the node's data at creation time, then on a timeout re-listing children and looking for a node
already carrying that identifier before ever calling create() again.
the session expires mid-wait
onSessionExpired is a HARD SIGNAL, not a retryable error: every ephemeral node and every watch that session owned is already
gone server-side by the time it fires. The correct response is starting over with a fresh acquire() on a new session, never
assuming any prior state - predecessor watches, the client's own myPath - is still valid.
Patterns, named - and one of them explains why this design needed no second server-side mechanism
Facade / Repository CoordinationClient hides the raw session and znode wire protocol; DistributedLock, LeaderElection and
MembershipGroup never talk to the network directly
Strategy ZkClient and EtcdClient are interchangeable behind one CoordinationClient interface
Observer, ONE-SHOT the watch mechanism IS the Observer pattern, deliberately weakened to fire once: subscribe, get
notified a single time, then explicitly re-subscribe. That one choice is what keeps notification
cost proportional to 'watchers active right now' rather than 'every watcher ever registered'.
State machine SessionState's one-way EXPIRED transition - a lifecycle as named states with enforced legal
transitions, never a boolean flag
Template method, LeaderElection and DistributedLock are the SAME sequential-node algorithm with a different
hiding in plain sight onBecomeLowest action - hold the lock, versus run as leader. Worth naming explicitly, because it is
the reason this design never needed two separate server-side mechanisms.
And the recipe generalizes further than 'one lock, one holder' once you are willing to interpret the ordered children list
differently: a READ-WRITE LOCK distinguishes nodes by a read-/write- prefix under the same path, where a writer still waits on
everyone ahead of it but a reader waits only on the WRITERS ahead of it - so the loop filters sortedChildren by prefix instead
of taking the single immediate predecessor.
